title: the sounds
hook: one puff of breath turns a hand into something harsh
tomorrow: it's Nani's birthday. why doesn't she need to read the card?

segments.voice: Yesterday, the sounds as a map of the mouth, throat to lips, and karmani's curled-back n. Today, the breath behind them.

The same word can land two ways. Fine. Fine. One is a shrug, the other a slammed door, and the only difference is the air behind it. Sanskrit builds that into its letters. Kara can mean a hand. Add a puff of breath after the k, kha, and khara means harsh, rough. Hold a palm in front of your lips and say both: the second one hits your hand.

The grammarians call that puff the great breath, mahaprana; letters without it are the little breath, alpaprana. The rows of the mouth's map come in these pairs: ka and kha, ga and gha, ta and tha, pa and pha. The difference is small enough to miss, and big enough to change the meaning. The tradition cares about breath in speech for more than spelling. In the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna describes a discipline of speech: words that cause no agitation, that are true, pleasant and beneficial, along with the regular recitation of sacred texts. It's a demanding list, because all of it has to be true at once. True, but also kind. Kind, but also useful. Not true and sharp; not pleasant and empty. And look how close harsh sits to a hand. The same two hands that hold out a cup can push. The same word, said with an extra rush of air, becomes the slammed door. When something goes out with too much breath behind it, a text, a comment, a reply in a group chat, the Gita's list doesn't scold. It gives a shape to try again: true, and gentle, and for the other person's good.

segments.voice: Hold your palm a few inches from your lips and say ka, then kha, and feel the second one land on your skin. Then rest the hand in your lap and breathe out as softly as you can, with no puff at all. Stay with that gentle out-breath, and let whatever you need to say next take its time.
The sounds: some made with a little breath, some with a great one, and a word that changes with the puff.
Carry this: the sounds, where a single puff of breath can turn a hand into something harsh. Go gently.

howItsDone: Teachers of Sanskrit and Hindi often have students hold a hand or a slip of paper before the mouth to feel the difference between unaspirated and aspirated consonants such as ka and kha.

alpaprana.meaning: little breath: a consonant said without a puff

notes: Answers 1439's question. Gita 17.15: anudvega-karaṃ vākyaṃ satyaṃ priya-hitaṃ ca yat, svādhyāyābhyasanaṃ caiva, vāṅmayaṃ tapa ucyate; paraphrased as speech that causes no agitation, true, pleasant and beneficial, with regular recitation. Confirm.
